patient.name: Brian Kowalczyk
patient.setting: GP surgery, neurology clinic, then a medical ward
patient.complaint: Shaking of his right hand and feeling 'slowed down' for 9 months
background: Retired bus driver in Lewisham; lives with his wife, Maureen
Lost his sense of smell 'years ago'

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an asymmetric resting pill-rolling tremor, bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity. Distractors: essential tremor (symmetrical, action), drug-induced parkinsonism, MSA, PSP, Lewy body dementia. Also asked: which drug made it worse, and on-off or dyskinesia complications.

points: Brian, 67: right hand shakes **at rest**, e.g. watching TV.
Shaking settles when he reaches for his cup.
Buttons and handwriting are slow; writing gets **smaller**.
Maureen: he **shouts and kicks in his sleep**.

steps.lead: Brian's slow movements and tremor come from **dopamine deficiency** in the basal ganglia, after loss of neurons in the **substantia nigra**.

points: Right wrist: **cogwheel** rigidity, worse when he moves the other hand.
Finger taps get smaller and slower (bradykinesia).
Reduced facial expression; reduced right arm swing; shuffling steps.

steps.lead: Brian has **TRAP**: resting tremor, rigidity, akinesia and early postural change, all **asymmetrical**: classic idiopathic Parkinson's.

visual.title: Tremor frequency
visual.label: Brian 4 Hz
visual.caption: Slow, resting and one-sided: Parkinson's. Faster, postural and symmetrical: essential tremor.

steps.lead: Brian's lost sense of smell and **dream enactment** (REM sleep behaviour disorder) came years before the tremor: classic early, non-motor clues.

steps.q: Which feature most strongly separates Brian's tremor from essential tremor?
steps.r: Parkinson's tremor is **resting and asymmetric**. Essential tremor is postural or action, symmetrical, often familial and eased by alcohol.

steps.title: Parkinson's or a lookalike?
head: Condition
Clue
rows: Asymmetric resting tremor, good levodopa response
Early severe autonomic failure: postural hypotension, falls
Vertical gaze palsy, early backward falls
Dementia within a year of motor signs, hallucinations

steps.lead: Brian's tremor is one-sided and his standing BP barely drops, so **MSA** and drug-induced parkinsonism are unlikely.

steps.text: **Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and haloperidol** are dopamine antagonists. In a stem with new parkinsonism, check the drug chart first.

steps.lead: Over years Brian may develop **on-off** fluctuations, dyskinesia, falls and dementia: the complications to watch for.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate next step?' (urgent referral to a specialist; the diagnosis is clinical) and 'Which investigation if the diagnosis is uncertain?' (DaTSCAN).

steps.q: The GP suspects Parkinson's. What is the most appropriate next step?
steps.r: Parkinson's is a **clinical diagnosis** by a specialist. NICE says refer **untreated**, so no levodopa before the neurologist sees him.

steps.lead: Brian's diagnosis is made **clinically** in the movement disorder clinic. No blood test or routine scan confirms it.

steps.text: A normal CT or MRI head does not rule Parkinson's out. Imaging is only to exclude other causes, e.g. vascular parkinsonism.

points: His brother, 70, has a symmetrical shake when holding a newspaper.
Neurologist unsure: tremor with **no clear bradykinesia**.

steps.lead: If the picture is unclear (e.g. Parkinson's vs essential tremor), a **DaTSCAN** shows reduced dopamine transporter uptake in Parkinson's.

visual.title: DaTSCAN striatal uptake (% of normal)
visual.label: Brian's left putamen 45%
visual.caption: Loss is worst on the side opposite the tremor. A normal scan points to essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism.

steps.text: DaTSCAN cannot separate Parkinson's from MSA or PSP: all three lose presynaptic dopamine neurones.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (levodopa with a decarboxylase inhibitor if function is impaired), the drug for wearing-off, the antiemetic (domperidone), nil by mouth (rotigotine patch), hallucinations (quetiapine) and never haloperidol.

points: Brian has dropped his cup twice; dressing takes 40 minutes.

steps.q: Brian's motor symptoms impair his daily function. What is first line?
o: Ropinirole in someone with gambling problems
steps.r: **Levodopa with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor** when function is impaired. Dopamine agonists are for milder symptoms and are avoided with impulse control problems.

steps.lead: Brian starts **co-careldopa**. Had his symptoms been mild, a **dopamine agonist** or **MAO-B inhibitor** could start, watching for impulse control disorders.

visual.title: Brian's mobility after 4 years on levodopa
visual.caption: Good after each dose, then 'off' before the next: **wearing-off**.

steps.lead: For Brian's **wearing-off**, levodopa is given **more often**, or an add-on (**entacapone**, an MAO-B inhibitor or an agonist) smooths the fluctuations.

points: Age 73: admitted with pneumonia; vomiting, **nil by mouth**.
Ward gave **metoclopramide**; he is now rigid and cannot turn in bed.
His 2 pm levodopa dose was missed.

steps.title: Admission bloods
steps.text: Infection plus missed doses and a dopamine antagonist: a recipe for acute deterioration.

steps.lead: Brian's levodopa is **time-critical**: it must be given on time, and never stopped because he is acutely unwell.

steps.title: Brian is nil by mouth
nodes: Ask the Parkinson's team or pharmacist
Restart oral levodopa as soon as safe

steps.lead: His sudden immobility is a **medication failure**. **Domperidone** replaces metoclopramide; if he becomes psychotic, **quetiapine**; if sedation is needed, **lorazepam**, never haloperidol.
Brian's care follows **NICE NG71**: specialist diagnosis, levodopa for impairing symptoms, and time-critical medicines in hospital.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: where the neurones are lost (substantia nigra pars compacta), the hallmark (Lewy bodies, alpha-synuclein), why carbidopa is added, and why dopamine antagonists or pulsatile levodopa cause trouble.

steps.title: Nigrostriatal failure
nodes: Substantia nigra pars compacta neurones die

steps.lead: Brian's slowness is the **indirect pathway winning**: too little nigrostriatal dopamine leaves the brake on movement.
If Brian's brain were examined, the hallmark would be **Lewy bodies**: clumps of **alpha-synuclein** inside neurones.

steps.q: What are Lewy bodies made of?
steps.r: **Alpha-synuclein**. Amyloid plaques and tau tangles are Alzheimer's; tau is also PSP.

steps.lead: Brian's **right-sided** tremor reflects more cell loss in the **left** nigra early on. Symmetry would point to MSA or a drug cause.
Metoclopramide **blocked the few dopamine receptors** Brian's depleted striatum had left: why he seized up on the ward.
Brian's wearing-off and dyskinesia come from **pulsatile** levodopa: receptors swing between flooded and empty instead of steady stimulation.

steps.title: Why each drug works
head: Drug
Mechanism
rows: Blocks peripheral DOPA decarboxylase, so more levodopa reaches the brain
Dopamine antagonist that does not cross the BBB

steps.text: Carbidopa does not cross the blood-brain barrier. It stops levodopa turning into dopamine **in the blood**, cutting nausea and postural hypotension.

mcq.q: What are the four cardinal features of Parkinson's disease (TRAP)?
mcq.r: **TRAP**: resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, akinesia/bradykinesia, postural instability.

mcq.q: What is the frequency of a parkinsonian tremor?
Which sleep disorder is an early feature of Parkinson's?
mcq.r: **REM sleep behaviour disorder** (dream enactment), with anosmia, can precede motor signs.

mcq.q: Which feature suggests multiple system atrophy rather than Parkinson's?
mcq.r: MSA: **early severe autonomic failure** (postural hypotension, falls, constipation).
A **clinical diagnosis** after urgent referral to a movement disorder specialist.

mcq.q: Which test helps when the diagnosis is uncertain?
What is first-line treatment when motor symptoms impair function?
mcq.r: **Levodopa plus a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor** (co-careldopa or co-beneldopa).

mcq.q: Which antiemetic is preferred in Parkinson's?
mcq.r: **Domperidone** does not cross the BBB; the others worsen parkinsonism.

mcq.q: Which drug class has the highest risk of impulse control disorders?
What is the pathological hallmark of Parkinson's disease?

prompts.q: What are the motor features of Parkinson's disease (TRAP), with the details examiners want?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: asymmetric resting tremor is the clincher.

points.p: Resting, pill-rolling tremor, 3–5 Hz, improves with movement

points.why: Rigidity plus tremor gives the cogwheel feel.

points.p: Postural instability: shuffling, stooped, festinant gait

points.why: Symmetry suggests essential tremor, drugs or MSA.

prompts.q: Which non-motor features can come before the motor signs?

points.p: REM sleep behaviour disorder: dream enactment
Autonomic dysfunction comes later in PD

prompts.q: How do you tell Parkinson's from essential tremor, drug-induced parkinsonism and MSA?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: symmetry, drug chart and autonomic features.

points.p: MSA: severe early autonomic failure, postural hypotension, falls
Drugs that worsen PD: metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, droperidol, haloperidol

prompts.q: What are the long-term complications of Parkinson's?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: time a symptom against the dose.

points.why: Dementia within a year of motor signs suggests Lewy body dementia.

prompts.q: How is Parkinson's diagnosed, and when is a DaTSCAN used?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: no test confirms classic PD.

points.p: Urgent referral to a movement disorder specialist, untreated
DaTSCAN if uncertain: reduced dopamine transporter uptake

prompts.q: What is first-line treatment, and which drugs are used for mild symptoms?

points.why: Highest risk of impulse control disorders.

points.p: Levodopa side effects: postural hypotension, dyskinesia, dystonia

prompts.q: How do you manage wearing-off and motor fluctuations?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: smooth the levodopa curve.

points.p: Add COMT inhibitor (entacapone), MAO-B inhibitor or dopamine agonist

prompts.q: What are the rules for Parkinson's patients in hospital?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: time-critical, safe antiemetic, safe antipsychotic.

points.p: Medicines are time-critical: never stop or delay
Nil by mouth: transdermal rotigotine patch

prompts.q: Explain the pathophysiology and pathology of Parkinson's.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the nucleus, the pathway and the protein.

points.p: Loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta
Direct pathway under-active, indirect over-active: bradykinesia, rigidity
Asymmetric neuronal loss explains asymmetric signs
points.why: Symptoms are opposite the worse nigra.

prompts.q: Why do carbidopa, dopamine antagonists and long-term levodopa have the effects they do?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: explain the drug effect in the vignette.

points.p: Dopamine antagonists block receptors in the depleted striatum
Long-term levodopa: pulsatile, non-physiological stimulation causes fluctuations

glossary.Parkinson's disease: Progressive neurodegeneration of dopamine neurones causing tremor, rigidity and slowness.
glossary.Parkinsonism: The movement pattern of tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia from any cause.
glossary.Substantia nigra: Midbrain nucleus whose dopamine neurones project to the striatum.
glossary.pars compacta: Part of the substantia nigra containing the dopaminergic neurones lost in Parkinson's.
glossary.Basal ganglia: Deep brain nuclei that control the initiation and scaling of movement.
glossary.Striatum: Caudate and putamen; receives dopamine from the substantia nigra.
glossary.Nigrostriatal pathway: Dopamine pathway from the substantia nigra to the striatum.
glossary.TRAP: Tremor, rigidity, akinesia and postural instability: the cardinal features of Parkinson's.
glossary.Pill-rolling: Resting tremor where thumb and fingers rub as if rolling a pill.
glossary.Cogwheel rigidity: Jerky, ratchet-like resistance to passive movement from rigidity plus tremor.
glossary.Bradykinesia: Slowness of movement with progressive loss of amplitude on repetition.
glossary.Hypomimia: Reduced facial expression, a mask-like face.
glossary.Micrographia: Small handwriting that shrinks across the page.
glossary.Festination: Short, quickening steps as if chasing the centre of gravity.
glossary.Anosmia: Loss of the sense of smell.
glossary.REM sleep behaviour disorder: Acting out dreams (shouting, kicking) because normal REM paralysis is lost.
glossary.Essential tremor: Familial, symmetrical postural and action tremor without bradykinesia.
glossary.Multiple system atrophy: Alpha-synuclein disease with parkinsonism and severe early autonomic failure.
glossary.PSP: Progressive supranuclear palsy: parkinsonism with vertical gaze palsy and early falls.
glossary.Lewy bodies: Intracellular clumps of alpha-synuclein; the pathological hallmark of Parkinson's.
glossary.Alpha-synuclein: Neuronal protein that misfolds and aggregates into Lewy bodies.
glossary.DaTSCAN: SPECT scan of dopamine transporters in the striatum; reduced in Parkinson's.
glossary.Levodopa: Dopamine precursor that crosses the blood-brain barrier; the most effective Parkinson's drug.
glossary.Carbidopa: Peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor given with levodopa.
glossary.Benserazide: Peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor combined with levodopa as co-beneldopa.
glossary.Dopamine agonists: Drugs that stimulate dopamine receptors directly, such as ropinirole and rotigotine.
glossary.Ropinirole: Oral dopamine agonist for Parkinson's and restless legs.
glossary.Rotigotine: Dopamine agonist given as a skin patch; used when patients are nil by mouth.
glossary.MAO-B inhibitor: Drug such as selegiline or rasagiline that slows dopamine breakdown in the brain.
glossary.COMT inhibitor: Drug such as entacapone that slows peripheral levodopa breakdown and prolongs each dose.
glossary.Entacapone: COMT inhibitor added to levodopa for wearing-off.
glossary.Impulse control disorders: Compulsive gambling, shopping, eating or hypersexuality, mostly from dopamine agonists.
glossary.Wearing-off: Return of Parkinson's symptoms before the next levodopa dose is due.
glossary.On-off phenomenon: Swings between good mobility (on) and immobility (off) on long-term levodopa.
glossary.Dyskinesia: Involuntary writhing or jerking movements, typically at peak levodopa levels.
glossary.Dystonia: Sustained muscle contraction causing twisting or abnormal postures.
glossary.Domperidone: Antiemetic dopamine antagonist that does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
glossary.Metoclopramide: Centrally acting dopamine-antagonist antiemetic that worsens parkinsonism.
glossary.Quetiapine: Atypical antipsychotic used first line for hallucinations in Parkinson's.
glossary.Haloperidol: Typical antipsychotic dopamine antagonist; contraindicated in Parkinson's.
glossary.Time-critical: Medicines that must be given within a set time of the scheduled dose to avoid harm.
glossary.NG71: NICE guideline on Parkinson's disease in adults.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man has a 1 year history of a tremor of his left hand. It is most noticeable when his hand rests in his lap and improves when he picks up a cup. He has become slower getting dressed. There is cogwheel rigidity at the left wrist and reduced left arm swing. His wife says he has lost his sense of smell.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: decide what type of tremor it is.

clues: most noticeable when his hand rests
improves when he picks up a cup
steps.x: Asymmetric resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity and anosmia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Parkinson's disease**.

elim: Drug-induced parkinsonism is symmetrical and needs a dopamine antagonist in the history.
Essential tremor is a symmetrical action tremor without rigidity or bradykinesia.
MSA has severe early autonomic failure and is often atremulous.
PSP has vertical gaze palsy and early backward falls.

steps.x: **D. Parkinson's disease.** Asymmetric rest tremor + bradykinesia = idiopathic Parkinson's.

technique.stem: A 69 year old woman has a 6 month history of a resting tremor of her right hand and slowness when walking. Examination shows bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity on the right. She is otherwise well and on no regular medicines.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: It asks how to confirm the diagnosis.

clues: resting tremor of her right hand
steps.x: Classic, untreated, not drug-induced Parkinson's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical diagnosis by a specialist: **urgent neurology referral**.

elim: CT does not confirm Parkinson's.
DaTSCAN is only for diagnostic uncertainty; this is classic.
MRI is normal in Parkinson's and does not confirm it.
NICE: refer before starting treatment.

steps.x: **E. Urgent referral to a neurologist.** Parkinson's is clinical; refer untreated.

technique.stem: A 76 year old man with Parkinson's disease has a 3 day history of seeing people in his bedroom who are not there. They frighten him. He takes co-careldopa. There is no infection or metabolic cause found and his medicines have been reviewed by the Parkinson's team.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment?

steps.x: Drug for psychosis in Parkinson's, after causes and medicines are reviewed.

clues: seeing people in his bedroom who are not there
steps.x: Distressing hallucinations, reversible causes excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Quetiapine**.

elim: Typical antipsychotics block dopamine and worsen Parkinson's.
Haloperidol is contraindicated in Parkinson's.
Metoclopramide is an antiemetic and a dopamine antagonist.
A dopamine agonist would worsen hallucinations.

steps.x: **D. Quetiapine.** PD psychosis = quetiapine; never haloperidol.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man dies of pneumonia. He had a 10 year history of Parkinson's disease. Post-mortem examination of his brainstem shows pallor of the substantia nigra and round eosinophilic inclusions inside the remaining neurones.
technique.q: What are these inclusions mainly composed of?

steps.x: It asks what the inclusion is made of.

clues: eosinophilic inclusions inside the remaining neurones
steps.x: Intracellular inclusions in nigral neurones = **Lewy bodies**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lewy bodies are **alpha-synuclein**.

elim: Amyloid-beta forms extracellular plaques in Alzheimer's.
Huntingtin aggregates are Huntington's disease.
Prion protein is CJD.
Tau tangles are Alzheimer's and PSP.

steps.x: **A. Alpha-synuclein.** Parkinson's hallmark = Lewy bodies = alpha-synuclein.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has a 9 month history of shaking of his right hand when watching television. His handwriting has become small. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg lying and 132/82 mmHg standing. There is a 4 Hz pill-rolling tremor of the right hand at rest and slowness of finger tapping on the right.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: An asymmetric 3–5 Hz resting pill-rolling tremor with bradykinesia and micrographia is Parkinson's disease. Essential tremor is symmetrical and postural; MSA has early autonomic failure.

steps.x: Diagnosis: characterise the tremor and look for bradykinesia.

clues: slowness of finger tapping on the right
steps.x: Asymmetric 4 Hz resting tremor, micrographia, bradykinesia, no autonomic failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Parkinson's disease**.

elim: Essential tremor is postural, faster and symmetrical.
Huntington's causes chorea, not a resting tremor.
MSA would show a large postural BP drop.
Wilson's affects young people with liver disease.

steps.x: **D. Parkinson's disease.** Asymmetric rest tremor + bradykinesia = PD.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man has noticed a tremor of his left hand. His wife says that for several years he has shouted and punched out in his sleep as if acting out his dreams. On examination there is a resting tremor of the left hand.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his left arm?
practice.e: REM sleep behaviour disorder and an asymmetric resting tremor suggest Parkinson's; the tone finding is cogwheel rigidity. Clasp-knife spasticity is an upper motor neurone sign.

steps.x: Most likely examination finding in suspected Parkinson's.

clues: shouted and punched out in his sleep
resting tremor of the left hand
steps.x: REM sleep behaviour disorder plus a resting tremor: Parkinson's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cogwheel rigidity**.

elim: Clasp-knife spasticity is an upper motor neurone sign.
Fasciculations suggest motor neurone disease.
Intention tremor is cerebellar.
Reflexes are normal in Parkinson's.

steps.x: **B. Cogwheel rigidity.** PD tone = cogwheel (rigidity plus tremor).

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman with Parkinson's disease is admitted with vomiting from gastroenteritis. Two days later she has become much stiffer and slower and cannot get out of bed. She has received her usual co-careldopa on time. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 124/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which drug is most likely to have caused her deterioration?
practice.e: Metoclopramide is a central dopamine antagonist and worsens parkinsonism. Domperidone does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so it is the antiemetic of choice.

steps.x: Which drug caused the parkinsonian deterioration?

clues: received her usual co-careldopa on time
steps.x: Doses are on time, so look for a dopamine-blocking antiemetic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metoclopramide**.

elim: Cyclizine is an antihistamine antiemetic and does not block dopamine.
Domperidone does not cross the BBB.
Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist and safe in Parkinson's.
Paracetamol does not affect dopamine.

steps.x: **C. Metoclopramide.** Antiemetic in PD: domperidone yes, metoclopramide no.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has had Parkinson's disease for 8 years and takes co-careldopa. About an hour after each dose he has writhing, twisting movements of his arms and trunk. They settle before his next dose.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
practice.e: Involuntary writhing movements an hour after levodopa, after years of treatment, are peak-dose dyskinesia from pulsatile stimulation. Wearing-off is the opposite: off symptoms before the next dose.

steps.x: It asks what the timed movements are.

clues: About an hour after each dose
steps.x: Involuntary movements at peak levodopa level after years of treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Peak-dose dyskinesia**.

elim: Akathisia is inner restlessness, often from antipsychotics.
Essential tremor is a rhythmic action tremor.
Huntington's chorea is not timed to doses.
Wearing-off is stiffness and slowness before the next dose.

steps.x: **D. Peak-dose dyskinesia.** Movements at peak = dyskinesia; slowness before the dose = wearing-off.

practice.stem: A 67 year old woman has had Parkinson's disease for 6 years. She takes co-careldopa three times a day. For the last 3 months she has become stiff, slow and tremulous about an hour before each dose is due. She improves within 30 minutes of each dose. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
practice.e: End-of-dose return of symptoms that improves with the next dose is wearing-off, a motor fluctuation of long-term levodopa. Peak-dose dyskinesia happens at the top of the curve.

steps.x: Explain symptoms timed to the end of a dose.

clues: about an hour before each dose is due
improves within 30 minutes of each dose
steps.x: Off symptoms at trough levels.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Wearing-off** (an on-off motor fluctuation).

elim: She is on no dopamine antagonist.
MSA responds poorly to levodopa and has autonomic failure.
NPH causes gait apraxia, incontinence and dementia.
Dyskinesia occurs at peak levels, not before a dose.

steps.x: **E. Wearing-off.** Off before the dose = wearing-off: give levodopa more often.

practice.stem: A 73 year old woman has a 2 year history of a resting tremor of her left hand and slowness doing up buttons. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg lying and 130/76 mmHg standing. There is cogwheel rigidity at the left wrist. She is asked to walk along the corridor.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her gait?
o: Shuffling gait with reduced arm swing
practice.e: Parkinson's gait is shuffling and stooped with reduced arm swing (often worse on the affected side) and festination. Broad-based gait is cerebellar; scissoring is spastic.

steps.x: Most likely gait finding in suspected Parkinson's.

clues: resting tremor of her left hand
steps.x: Asymmetric resting tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity: Parkinson's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Shuffling gait with reduced arm swing**.

elim: A broad-based gait is cerebellar.
High-stepping is foot drop from a peripheral nerve lesion.
Scissoring is spastic diplegia, an upper motor neurone sign.
Waddling is proximal myopathy.

steps.x: **D. Shuffling gait with reduced arm swing.** PD gait: short shuffling steps, stooped, reduced arm swing, festination.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man has a tremor of both hands, worse when holding a cup. His neurologist cannot decide whether he has mild bradykinesia. He is on no regular medicines. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to help confirm Parkinson's disease?
practice.e: When it is unclear whether a tremor is parkinsonian, a DaTSCAN shows reduced striatal dopamine transporter uptake in Parkinson's and is normal in essential tremor.

steps.x: It asks for a test when the clinical diagnosis is uncertain.

clues: cannot decide whether he has mild bradykinesia
steps.x: Uncertain: Parkinson's versus essential tremor.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **DaTSCAN**.

elim: CT does not show dopaminergic loss.
EEG is for seizures.
Caeruloplasmin tests for Wilson's disease in young patients.
TFTs exclude a thyrotoxic tremor but do not confirm Parkinson's.

steps.x: **B. DaTSCAN.** Uncertain PD vs essential tremor = DaTSCAN.

practice.stem: A 69 year old woman with suspected Parkinson's disease has a DaTSCAN because her diagnosis is uncertain. She has a resting tremor of her right hand.
practice.q: Which is the most likely DaTSCAN finding?
o: Reduced uptake in the left striatum
Reduced uptake in the right striatum
practice.e: Parkinson's shows reduced dopamine transporter uptake in the striatum, worst on the side opposite the symptoms because of asymmetric nigral loss.

steps.x: It asks what the scan shows, and on which side.

clues: resting tremor of her right hand
steps.x: Right-sided signs come from the left basal ganglia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Reduced uptake in the left striatum**.

elim: Uptake is reduced, not increased.
A normal scan suggests essential tremor or drug-induced parkinsonism.
DaTSCAN images the striatum, not the cerebellum.
The tremor is right-sided, so the left (contralateral) striatum is worse.

steps.x: **D. Reduced uptake in the left striatum.** DaTSCAN: reduced, worst opposite the symptoms.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has Parkinson's disease diagnosed by a neurologist. His tremor and slowness now make it difficult to dress and eat. He has no history of gambling or other impulse control problems.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: When motor symptoms impair quality of life, levodopa with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (co-careldopa) is first line. MAO-B inhibitors or agonists suit mild symptoms.

steps.x: Initial drug when motor symptoms impair function.
Diagnosed PD with significant functional impairment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Co-careldopa** (levodopa + carbidopa).

elim: Entacapone is an add-on for motor fluctuations, not used alone.
Haloperidol worsens parkinsonism.
Propranolol helps essential tremor, not bradykinesia.
MAO-B inhibitors are an option for mild symptoms only.

steps.x: **A. Co-careldopa.** Impairing motor symptoms = levodopa + decarboxylase inhibitor.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman with Parkinson's disease is admitted with pneumonia. She is vomiting and needs an antiemetic. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 126/74 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate antiemetic?
practice.e: Domperidone is the antiemetic of choice because it does not cross the blood-brain barrier. Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and haloperidol block central dopamine receptors.

steps.x: Pick a safe antiemetic for Parkinson's.
Avoid any centrally acting dopamine antagonist.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Domperidone**.

elim: Haloperidol is contraindicated in Parkinson's.
Metoclopramide crosses the BBB and worsens parkinsonism.
Prochlorperazine is a central dopamine antagonist.
Promethazine is a phenothiazine and best avoided.

steps.x: **A. Domperidone.** PD antiemetic = domperidone.

practice.stem: A 78 year old man with Parkinson's disease is admitted after a stroke. His swallow assessment shows he is unsafe to take anything by mouth. He normally takes co-careldopa four times a day. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate way to continue his Parkinson's treatment?
o: Omit all Parkinson's medicines until he can swallow
practice.e: Parkinson's medicines are time-critical; if oral levodopa cannot be taken a transdermal dopamine agonist (rotigotine) patch is used. Omitting doses risks acute deterioration.

practice.q: Which is the mechanism of action of carbidopa?
o: Blocks dopamine receptors in the gut
practice.e: Carbidopa blocks peripheral DOPA decarboxylase, so more levodopa reaches the brain and peripheral side effects (nausea, hypotension) fall. Entacapone inhibits COMT.
